case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) authorizes the President to impose import tariffs as an emergency economic measure.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) (IEEPA) (and, in the consolidated merits briefing referenced, the related constitutional nondelegation/separation-of-powers issue if IEEPA is construed to allow tariffs).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (importers challenging the duties) argue that IEEPA’s grant of authority to “regulate…importation” and to “investigate, regulate, or prohibit” certain transactions does not include the distinct congressional power to levy tariffs (taxes/duties on imports). They emphasize the traditional constitutional and statutory separation between (a) emergency controls/sanctions over transactions and property and (b) revenue-raising customs duties set by Congress through the tariff laws and specialized trade statutes. On their view, reading IEEPA to allow tariffs would (1) contradict IEEPA’s structure and history, (2) improperly let the President bypass trade statutes that contain detailed procedural and substantive limits, and (3) raise serious separation-of-powers/nondelegation concerns—so the Court should interpret IEEPA narrowly to avoid those constitutional problems. Petitioners also resist transfer/redirecting the litigation as a way to avoid prompt merits review, arguing the dispute arises under IEEPA as the substantive source of authority challenged.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (the President and federal government, as reflected in the cited hearing excerpts and the pro-government amici alignment in the consolidated posture) maintain that IEEPA’s text is broad and flexible in emergencies and includes power to ‘regulate…importation’—a phrase they contend can encompass imposing duties as a regulatory tool. They further argue that courts should not second-guess the President’s emergency determinations (e.g., whether an ‘unusual and extraordinary threat’ exists) because those determinations are committed to the political branches and are effectively nonjusticiable under doctrines like the political question doctrine. Procedurally, the government has also pressed jurisdiction/venue arguments that the challenge belongs in the Court of International Trade (CIT) under the customs/trade jurisdictional scheme, rather than in a district court/ordinary APA-style path, and suggests that courts need not reach merits before transferring. In the consolidated Supreme Court posture (Nos. 24-1287 & 25-250), the government also seeks resolution of an alternative question: if IEEPA authorizes tariffs, whether that authorization is an unconstitutional delegation.
key_precedents: K Mart Corp. v. Cartier, Inc. (referenced in the jurisdiction discussion as a CIT/Federal Circuit-related authority)
BP p.l.c. v. Mayor and City Council of Baltimore, 593 U.S. 230 (quoted for limits on congressional "ratification" by reenactment or silence)

John Roberts.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that §1702(a)(1)(B)’s authority to “regulate…importation” is linguistically broad and, in emergencies, should be read flexibly—but the question is whether those general words clearly authorize an across-the-board customs duty, a quintessential Article I instrument that Congress has treated through detailed tariff statutes. Justice Alito’s major-questions/clear-statement framing most strengthens the narrow statutory disposition: we should not infer a sweeping tariff switch from IEEPA’s sanctions-oriented structure absent unmistakable clarity, especially given the economic significance and the risk of displacing Congress’s comprehensive trade scheme. Justice Gorsuch’s Youngstown point underscores why the narrower construction is institutionally sound: reading IEEPA to create a parallel tariff power would invite serious separation-of-powers and nondelegation concerns that we can avoid by holding simply that IEEPA does not authorize the imposition of general duties. BP p.l.c., as I noted, further blocks any ratification-by-silence theory; congressional inaction cannot supply the clear authorization the government needs here.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The respondent’s best textual point remains that § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “regulate … importation,” and that “regulate” can be read broadly enough to include exactions at the border. But as Justice Gorsuch and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize, tariffs are historically and constitutionally understood as “Duties” and “Imposts”—a distinct Article I instrument—and IEEPA’s surrounding text and structure target sanctions-style controls on transactions/property, not a general power to impose customs duties. Chief Justice Roberts’s reliance on BP p.l.c. is also persuasive against any ratification-by-silence theory: congressional inaction cannot supply a clear transfer of so fundamental a legislative power. Even if “regulate” can sometimes sweep widely, the original public meaning and statutory context counsel the narrower construction that avoids converting emergency authority into a substitute tariff code and thereby creating acute separation-of-powers/nondelegation concerns.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the textual breadth of “regulate…importation,” but that general phrase cannot plausibly be read to confer the quintessential Article I power to impose duties—especially where Congress has enacted detailed, trade-specific tariff regimes that would be effectively displaced. Chief Justice Roberts’s major-questions/clear-statement framing is persuasive on a statutory ground: if Congress meant IEEPA to operate as a nationwide tariff switch of vast economic consequence, it would have spoken far more clearly than by embedding a few broad words in an emergency sanctions statute. Justice Thomas’s structural point about “Duties” and “Imposts,” combined with Justice Gorsuch’s Youngstown analysis, reinforces that we should avoid a construction that would place the President in tension with Congress’s comprehensive tariff framework and invite serious nondelegation/separation-of-powers problems. BP p.l.c., as Roberts notes, further undercuts any ratification-by-silence theory, so I remain with the petitioner on a narrow statutory interpretation that treats IEEPA as authorizing sanctions-style import controls, not revenue-like tariffs.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that IEEPA’s power to “regulate…importation” is linguistically broad and, in an emergency, could be read to include a tariff-like exaction. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, statutory context and coherence matter: IEEPA is built around sanctions-style controls on transactions and property, and treating it as an implicit tariff statute would quietly displace Congress’s detailed customs and trade framework—precisely where we should demand a clear statement. Justice Gorsuch’s Youngstown framing reinforces that when Congress has comprehensively legislated on tariffs, we should not infer a parallel, economically sweeping duty power from general words, especially given BP p.l.c.’s caution against reading congressional silence as ratification. Given the regressive, real-world price impacts on consumers and small businesses, I remain unwilling to bless a de facto tariff authority absent unmistakable congressional authorization.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The respondent’s strongest textual point remains the capacious phrase “regulate…importation,” but read in IEEPA’s immediate company—foreign exchange, transfers of credit, and property interests—it most naturally authorizes sanctions-style controls (licensing, prohibitions, embargoes), not the distinct congressional instrument of generally applicable customs duties embedded in a comprehensive tariff code. Chief Justice Roberts’s clear-statement approach is persuasive on pragmatic textualist grounds: treating general emergency language as a latent tariff switch would create statutory incoherence across IEEPA and the detailed trade statutes Congress has enacted, and BP p.l.c. properly cautions against inferring ratification from congressional inaction. Justice Alito’s major-questions framing reinforces (rather than replaces) the textual/contextual reading by explaining why we should not locate an economically transformative tariff power in a few general words, especially where that construction would unnecessarily invite Youngstown/nondelegation concerns. Nothing in colleagues’ points undermines the core contextual-textual inference, so I remain with the petitioner.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains that § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “regulate…importation,” and in isolation that language is broad enough to reach border exactions. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett stress, statutory context matters: IEEPA’s design is sanctions-style control of transactions and property during emergencies, not a quiet transfer of Congress’s distinct Article I power to impose generally applicable customs duties that function like taxes within a comprehensive tariff code. Justice Alito’s clear-statement/major-questions point dovetails with that textual reading: if Congress meant to hand the President a sweeping nationwide tariff switch via emergency declaration, it would have spoken unmistakably, and BP p.l.c. (as Roberts notes) cuts against treating legislative silence as ratification of an extraordinary asserted power. Under Youngstown, the narrower construction best avoids turning IEEPA into a de facto tariff statute that collides with Congress’s detailed trade legislation and raises unnecessary separation-of-powers concerns.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The government’s best argument remains that IEEPA’s power to “regulate…importation” is linguistically broad and, in an emergency foreign-affairs setting, should include tariffs as a leverage tool. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, reading those general words to authorize across-the-board customs duties would quietly convert a sanctions/transactions statute into a sweeping Article I tariff power that Congress has historically exercised through detailed tariff legislation; under Justice Alito’s major-questions/clear-statement framing, that is precisely the kind of economically significant shift we do not infer from broad language. Justice Gorsuch’s Youngstown point further supports the narrow construction: given Congress’s comprehensive tariff scheme, the asserted power looks at least constitutionally doubtful absent clear authorization, so statutory avoidance counsels against the government’s reading. BP p.l.c., as Roberts notes, also undercuts any ratification-by-silence theory, leaving me satisfied that a narrow, institutional statutory holding for petitioner is the sound course.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The respondent’s best point remains the ordinary breadth of “regulate…importation,” which can include setting conditions at the border; but read in IEEPA’s immediate context—foreign-exchange, transfers, and property-interests controls—the phrase functions as sanctions-style authority (licensing, embargoes, restrictions), not an implicit delegation to impose general customs duties that operate as taxes. Chief Justice Roberts’s emphasis on statutory coherence and BP p.l.c.’s skepticism of ratification-by-silence strengthens my view that congressional inaction under the NEA cannot supply the clear authorization needed for a power Congress has otherwise treated as quintessentially legislative through detailed tariff statutes. Justice Alito’s major-questions/clear-statement framing and Justice Gorsuch’s Youngstown/Article I point together underscore that we should not read a sweeping, economically significant tariff switch into general emergency words when Congress has occupied the field in trade law. Nothing in the government’s breadth argument overcomes those textual and structural cues, so my vote remains for the petitioner.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The government’s best point remains the text’s breadth—IEEPA allows the President to “regulate…importation,” and in ordinary usage that could sweep in border conditions with economic bite. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, statutory context and coherence matter: IEEPA is built as a sanctions-and-transactions regime, and reading a few general words to authorize sweeping, revenue-like customs duties would silently displace Congress’s detailed tariff framework and reallocate core Article I power without a clear statement. Justice Alito’s major-questions/clear-statement framing reinforces my pragmatic concern about consequences: an emergency-triggered unilateral tariff switch would destabilize the trade system and reduce procedural accountability, and narrowing the statute avoids serious Youngstown Category 3 and nondelegation questions. BP p.l.c., as Roberts notes, further undercuts any ratification-by-silence argument, so the narrower construction remains the best fit and my vote stays with petitioner.

John Roberts.reasoning: IEEPA’s grant to “regulate … importation,” 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), is best read to authorize targeted transactional controls in an emergency, not the imposition of across-the-board customs duties—an area where Congress has traditionally spoken with specificity through the tariff and trade statutes. Given the economic and institutional significance of recognizing a unilateral presidential tariff power, we should hesitate to find such authority in a few general words and instead adopt the narrower interpretation that avoids serious separation-of-powers/nondelegation concerns. That approach respects Congress’s role over duties and preserves institutional legitimacy by deciding on statutory grounds without reaching a constitutional holding. As BP p.l.c. v. Mayor and City Council of Baltimore, 593 U.S. 230, cautions, we should not treat legislative silence or broad reenactment as ratification of an extraordinary asserted power.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Constitution assigns Congress the power to “lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises,” and IEEPA’s text, 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), authorizes the President to “regulate … importation” as an emergency control over transactions and property—not to impose revenue-raising customs duties absent a clear statement. Reading “regulate … importation” to include tariffs would allow the Executive to circumvent the detailed tariff and trade statutes Congress has enacted, and would raise serious separation-of-powers and nondelegation concerns; the better textual reading is the narrower one that avoids those constitutional difficulties. The government’s appeal to breadth and “emergency” flexibility cannot supply authority that Congress did not clearly confer, particularly where the claimed power is quintessentially legislative. Consistent with BP p.l.c. v. Mayor & City Council of Baltimore, 593 U.S. 230, I would not treat congressional silence or general language as ratifying an extraordinary presidential power to tax via tariffs.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: IEEPA’s text authorizes the President to “investigate, regulate, or prohibit” transactions and to “regulate…importation,” 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), but it does not clearly confer the distinct power to impose tariffs—an instrument historically tied to Congress’s revenue and trade regime and governed by detailed, separate tariff statutes. Reading “regulate…importation” to include nationwide duties of major economic and political significance would trigger the Court’s clear-statement expectations under the major questions doctrine, akin to Alabama Assn. of Realtors v. DHHS, where broad language could not support a sweeping economic measure. That narrowing construction also avoids serious separation-of-powers/nondelegation concerns if IEEPA were treated as a blank check for tariffs. Practical consequences reinforce this reading because it would allow the Executive to bypass the tailored procedural limits Congress built into specialized trade laws.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: IEEPA’s grant to “regulate… importation” in 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) is best read to authorize emergency controls on transactions and property, not the imposition of revenue-raising customs duties—an Article I power Congress has addressed through detailed tariff and trade statutes. Under Youngstown, the President may act only pursuant to clear congressional authorization, and construing IEEPA to permit tariffs would risk letting the Executive bypass Congress’s carefully cabined trade frameworks and raise serious separation-of-powers/nondelegation concerns, so the statute should be construed narrowly to avoid those constitutional problems. The government’s reliance on congressional inaction under the National Emergencies Act does not amount to affirmative authorization, and silence cannot do the work of ratification where the question is whether Congress delegated the power to tax. Given the real-world stakes for importers and consumers, especially vulnerable communities who bear regressive price impacts, courts should require unmistakable clarity before allowing emergency statutes to be used to impose broad tariffs.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: IEEPA’s text authorizes the President to “investigate, regulate, or prohibit” transactions and to “regulate…importation,” 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), but read in statutory context that language is best understood to permit emergency controls on dealings in property and cross-border transactions—not the imposition of revenue-raising customs duties that Congress has addressed through detailed, trade-specific tariff statutes. Treating “regulate…importation” as a tariff power would effect a major alteration of the tariff scheme and invite serious separation-of-powers/nondelegation concerns; a coherent, workable reading therefore construes IEEPA not to displace the tariff laws absent a clearer statement. That narrower construction respects statutory purpose (emergency economic controls tied to foreign threats) while avoiding an interpretation that would let the President bypass the procedural and substantive limits Congress built into specialized trade authorities. On the merits, the President’s emergency determinations may be owed deference, but the threshold question of statutory authorization is judicially reviewable and does not turn on political-question deference.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: IEEPA’s operative grant in 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) permits the President to “investigate, regulate, or prohibit” specified transactions and to “regulate…importation,” but nothing in its text clearly authorizes the quintessentially congressional act of imposing duties—taxes collected at the border—especially given Article I’s assignment to Congress of the power to “lay and collect Taxes, Duties, Imposts and Excises.” Under Justice Jackson’s Youngstown framework, the President’s claimed power to levy tariffs in the teeth of Congress’s detailed tariff statutes places this action at best in a zone where Congress has not clearly authorized it, and at worst where Congress has occupied the field—requiring a clear statement before we treat IEEPA as silently displacing the customary separation between sanctions-like controls and tariff legislation. Reading IEEPA to permit sweeping tariffs would also trigger serious separation-of-powers and nondelegation concerns, so the better textual reading is the narrower one that avoids those constitutional doubts. And congressional “silence” or later inaction cannot supply the missing authorization. (See BP p.l.c. v. Mayor & City Council of Baltimore, 593 U.S. 230).

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: IEEPA’s text, 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), authorizes the President to “regulate” or “prohibit” transactions involving property and to “regulate…importation,” but it does not clearly authorize the quintessential Article I power to impose revenue-raising customs duties; Congress has historically addressed tariffs through detailed trade statutes, and a major shift of that kind requires a clear statement. Under Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, the President has no independent authority to seize Congress’s enumerated economic powers, and any claimed tariffing authority must rest on a clear congressional delegation—especially where the alternative reading would let the President bypass the carefully reticulated tariff laws and raise serious separation-of-powers/nondelegation concerns. Given IEEPA’s history as a constraint on emergency economic powers and the practical workability/legitimacy concerns of allowing emergency proclamations to set nationwide tariff policy, I would construe IEEPA narrowly to avoid those constitutional problems. The government’s broad reading would effectively transfer the power to “lay and collect…Duties” from Congress to the President without sufficient guidance, contrary to structure and tradition.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: IEEPA’s operative grant—authority to “investigate, regulate, or prohibit” transactions and to “regulate…importation,” 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B)—is best read, in its original public meaning and statutory context, as empowering emergency controls over foreign-exchange and property-related transactions rather than authorizing the imposition of revenue-raising customs duties traditionally set through the tariff laws. Reading “regulate…importation” to include tariffs would allow the President to bypass Congress’s detailed trade statutes and thereby place the President in Justice Jackson’s Youngstown Category 3 when Congress has occupied the field with specific tariff mechanisms, making such a construction methodologically suspect absent a clear statement. That broad reading would also trigger serious separation-of-powers/nondelegation concerns, reinforcing the narrower construction under the avoidance canon. Youngstown confirms that presidential power to act domestically with economic consequences must “stem either from an act of Congress or from the Constitution itself,” and the text here is not clear enough to shift the tariff power from Congress to the Executive.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: IEEPA’s text, 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), authorizes the President to “investigate, regulate, or prohibit” certain transactions and to “regulate…importation,” but that emergency-control language is best read to cover sanctions-style restrictions on property and transactions—not the distinct congressional power to impose revenue-raising customs duties. Construing “regulate…importation” to include tariffs would effectively allow the President to bypass Congress’s detailed trade and tariff schemes and would thrust this case into Youngstown’s third category, where presidential action is least supportable because it intrudes upon an area of traditional and specifically legislated congressional control. Reading IEEPA to allow tariffs would also trigger serious separation-of-powers/nondelegation concerns, so a narrower construction that avoids those constitutional problems is the more procedurally fair and practically workable interpretation. The government’s broad foreign-affairs framing (including reliance on Curtiss-Wright-style deference) cannot overcome the requirement that executive power here must be grounded in a clear statutory authorization when Congress has legislated comprehensively in the field.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), specifically 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B), authorizes the President to impose tariffs (and, in the consolidated merits posture, whether such authority would be an unconstitutional delegation if it exists).
case_analysis.legal_provision: 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) (IEEPA grant of power to regulate/affect certain economic transactions during a declared national emergency); also implicated: U.S. Const. art. I (Congress’s taxing and tariff powers) and separation-of-powers/nondelegation principles (raised in No. 25-250).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners (Learning Resources, et al.) argue that IEEPA’s text and structure do not confer tariff-setting power: it authorizes the President to regulate specified transactions involving foreign exchange, banking transfers, and property interests to address an emergency, but does not speak in the distinct, traditionally congressional language of imposing customs duties. They emphasize that tariffs are a form of tax/duty historically and constitutionally assigned to Congress, and that reading IEEPA to permit tariffs would improperly convert a targeted emergency economic-controls statute into a broad revenue/trade instrument—something Congress has addressed separately through detailed tariff statutes. Petitioners also resist attempts to avoid merits review through forum/venue transfer to the Court of International Trade, contending the case ‘arises under’ IEEPA (not the tariff schedule) and therefore belongs in ordinary federal court; they point to authority such as K Mart to rebut exclusivity arguments for the CIT.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents (the President and federal officials) contend that IEEPA’s broad operational verbs—especially authority to ‘regulate’ or ‘prohibit’ certain import-related or property-related transactions during a national emergency—are sufficiently capacious to encompass tariffs as a means of regulating importation/economic conduct in response to an ‘unusual and extraordinary threat.’ They further argue that challenges to the President’s compliance with IEEPA’s emergency predicates (e.g., whether a qualifying ‘unusual and extraordinary threat’ exists, adequacy of findings, fit of means to ends) are nonjusticiable political questions committed to the political branches by Congress’s emergency framework. On procedure, the government has pressed for transfer/exclusive jurisdiction in the Court of International Trade, seeking to have customs-related disputes funneled there; and in the consolidated posture (No. 25-250), the government also tees up the alternative: if IEEPA does authorize tariffs, it does not unconstitutionally delegate legislative power because emergency statutes supply an intelligible principle and are historically upheld in foreign-affairs/national-security contexts.
key_precedents: BP p.l.c. v. Mayor & City Council of Baltimore, 593 U.S. 230 (2021) (cited for skepticism about congressional ratification/reenactment as an interpretive tool absent settled precedent)
K Mart Corp. v. Cartier, Inc., 486 U.S. 281 (1988) (invoked regarding customs/CIT jurisdiction and review of trade-related actions)
Baker v. Carr, 369 U.S. 186 (1962) (background political question doctrine framework implicated by the government’s ‘political question’ argument)
J.W. Hampton, Jr. & Co. v. United States, 276 U.S. 394 (1928) (core intelligible-principle/nondelegation precedent relevant to the delegation question raised in No. 25-250)
Gundy v. United States, 588 U.S. 128 (2019) (modern nondelegation discussion relevant if the Court reaches the constitutional question)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s best point remains the TWEA pedigree and Yoshida’s reading of “regulate … importation” to permit an import surcharge, but that lower-court construction of a different statute in a different moment cannot substitute for a clear congressional statement when the Executive claims authority to impose what functionally operates as a tariff. As Justice Kagan emphasizes, IEEPA’s text and structure are sanctions- and property/transaction-control oriented, and treating it as a tariff statute would create serious mismatch with Congress’s detailed tariff codes—an interpretive signal that Congress did not silently transfer core Article I tariff-setting power. Even crediting the emergency predicates and reporting/termination tools Justice Kavanaugh cites, those political checks do not answer the threshold question of statutory meaning, and a narrow reading avoids unnecessary constitutional/nondelegation issues consistent with judicial minimalism. Yoshida therefore informs the background but does not overcome the absence of tariff/duty language and the major shift in allocation of authority that the government’s interpretation would effect.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point is the TWEA pedigree and Yoshida’s reading of “regulate … importation” to allow an import surcharge, but that backdrop cannot override IEEPA’s enacted text, which authorizes regulation/prohibition of transactions and property interests and nowhere uses the historically revenue-linked terms “duties” or “tariffs.” As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, treating IEEPA as a tariff statute would effect a major transfer of Article I authority without a clear textual indication; legislative history or congressional “awareness” of a lower-court decision is not an originalist substitute for statutory language. Even if “regulate importation” could linguistically sweep broadly, original public meaning in this constitutional setting requires clarity before we construe a sanctions tool as conferring tariff-setting power, especially given Congress’s detailed tariff statutes elsewhere. Accepting Respondent’s reading would also aggravate, not alleviate, the separation-of-powers/nondelegation concerns by implying an effectively standardless power to set rates under an emergency label.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s Yoshida/TWEA-lineage point is the most substantial rejoinder, but it ultimately asks us to treat a lower-court construction of a different statute as silently transporting an Article I tariff power into IEEPA without the tariff-specific words and mechanisms Congress routinely uses. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 1702(a)(1)(B) is framed in transactional/property-control verbs (“regulate” or “prohibit” dealings and interests), and converting that into authority to impose a revenue-raising border duty would be a major shift in the statutory scheme and the constitutional allocation that demands clearer textual evidence than “regulate importation” alone. Yoshida may show that “regulate” can be used broadly in wartime-era emergency legislation, but it does not overcome IEEPA’s post-TWEA purpose of cabining emergency economic powers and its conspicuous omission of duty/tariff terminology. The narrower reading also avoids turning IEEPA into a general trade-and-revenue instrument by executive decree, a practical and separation-of-powers consequence that reinforces—not replaces—the textual analysis.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s Yoshida/TWEA-lineage point is the best argument for the government, but it still does not justify reading IEEPA’s general phrase “regulate … importation” as silently granting tariff power: Yoshida was a lower-court construction of a different statute in a distinct historical setting, and “awareness” of that decision cannot substitute for the kind of clear, revenue-linked language Congress routinely uses when it authorizes duties. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, IEEPA’s structure is sanctions-like—blocking, licensing, and prohibiting transactions—and treating it as a tariff code would be a major shift in Article I allocation that triggers a clear-statement instinct under Youngstown-style separation-of-powers avoidance. On my pragmatic approach, the domestic incidence matters: allowing the Executive to impose border charges with sweeping consumer effects (often borne by vulnerable communities) is precisely why we should demand explicit congressional authorization before converting an emergency economic-controls statute into a trade-and-revenue instrument. Because the statutory text and structure resolve the case, I still would not reach nondelegation.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s strongest point remains the TWEA pedigree and Yoshida’s reading that “regulate … importation” can encompass an import surcharge, but that historical episode doesn’t overcome what Congress actually wrote in IEEPA—a transaction-and-property control statute that conspicuously lacks the duty/tariff/rate vocabulary and procedural signals Congress uses when it means to confer border-revenue authority. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, treating § 1702(a)(1)(B) as tariff power would make IEEPA structurally incoherent with the detailed tariff code and effectively allow the Executive to bypass the ordinary, accountable tariff-setting framework; that is a major statutory mismatch on a pragmatic textualist read. Yoshida (a lower-court construction of a different statute in a different context) may show semantic possibility, but it cannot supply the clear textual hook needed to convert “regulate” in this sanctions-style setting into a power to levy duties, especially given the constitutional shadow Justice Thomas flags. I therefore stay with the narrower reading that preserves statutory coherence and avoids silently reallocating core Article I tariff authority.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s best point is the TWEA lineage and Yoshida’s reading of “regulate … importation” to allow an import surcharge, but that lower-court construction of a different statute cannot supply the clear textual authorization IEEPA itself lacks—especially where Congress elsewhere speaks in the distinct terms of “duties” and “tariffs” when it means to confer revenue authority. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett emphasize, § 1702(a)(1)(B) is framed around regulating or prohibiting transactions and dealings in property interests, which naturally fits licensing, blocking, and embargo-like controls—not the imposition of a border charge functioning as a tariff. Accepting the government’s reading would effectively turn IEEPA into an all-purpose tariff code, triggering the separation-of-powers and Youngstown concerns Justice Thomas flags and confirming that the narrower construction is both the better textual fit and the constitutionally sounder path. I therefore remain with Petitioner and would resolve the case on statutory grounds without reaching nondelegation.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch make the best point that IEEPA does not employ the customary tariff/duty vocabulary and that we should hesitate before reading an emergency statute to shift core Article I tariff authority by implication. But I remain persuaded that § 1702(a)(1)(B)’s authorization to “regulate … importation … of … any property” is textually capacious, and the TWEA § 5(b) lineage—together with Yoshida’s contemporaneous construction of the same operative phrase—supplies strong historical evidence of the semantic scope Congress carried forward when it enacted IEEPA. Justice Thomas’s and Justice Barrett’s clear-statement framing rests on a judicially imposed magic-words requirement that is hard to reconcile with Congress’s choice of broad language and with the national-security predicates and political checks Congress built into IEEPA, which already cabin the delegation in a way that makes the major-questions/avoidance move less fitting here. I therefore would uphold the President’s action as within the statute, leaving any policy or institutional concerns to Congress’s amendment and oversight tools rather than narrowing the enacted text.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s best point remains that § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “regulate … importation … of … property,” and that TWEA § 5(b)’s similar language was read in Yoshida to permit an import surcharge. But Yoshida is a lower-court interpretation of a different statute, and even if it supplies some historical evidence of semantic breadth, it cannot substitute for what Congress actually enacted in IEEPA—whose operative verbs and surrounding structure are oriented to sanctions-style control of transactions and property interests, not the setting of border duties. As Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes, treating IEEPA as a tariff statute would effect a major shift in Article I-linked revenue authority, and under a textualist/originalist approach I would require a clear textual indication (the kind Congress uses elsewhere—duties, tariffs, rates, schedules) before attributing that power to § 1702. Because the statutory reading resolves the case, the national-security context and IEEPA’s political checks do not cure the delegation problem or justify reading “regulate importation” to include imposing a tariff-like charge absent clear statement.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Kavanaugh’s Yoshida/TWEA-lineage point is the strongest case for the government because it shows that similar “regulate importation” language has been read to encompass an import surcharge. But as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan stress, IEEPA’s enacted text and structure are oriented to sanctions-style control of transactions and property interests, and it lacks the customary tariff/duty/rate signals Congress uses when it truly delegates border-revenue authority—especially given the detailed tariff statutes that supply those procedures and accountability. Even if Congress was “aware” of Yoshida, that backdrop cannot do the clear-statement work needed to transform an emergency economic-controls statute into a general tariff instrument with major domestic consequences, and constitutional-avoidance/Youngstown concerns counsel the narrower construction. I therefore remain with the Petitioner on the statutory ground and would not reach nondelegation.

John Roberts.reasoning: IEEPA’s operative grant in 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “regulate” or “prohibit” specified transactions involving foreign exchange, transfers of credit or payments, and property interests, but it does not speak in the distinct terms Congress traditionally uses to confer tariff/duty authority, and we should not lightly read an emergency economic-controls statute to displace Congress’s Article I control over customs duties. Under Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, the President’s power must rest on clear statutory or constitutional footing; absent a clear authorization for tariffs, the claimed power is at best in Justice Jackson’s uncertain “zone of twilight,” and in practice risks sliding toward action Congress has not approved. A narrow, precedent-respecting disposition is therefore to hold that § 1702(a)(1)(B) does not authorize tariffs, avoiding the constitutional nondelegation question (cf. J.W. Hampton; Gundy) and preserving institutional legitimacy by deciding on the least disruptive ground. The government’s political-question framing is unpersuasive where the issue is the meaning of a statute—a classic judicial task—and not the wisdom of emergency policy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The text of 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “regulate” certain transactions and property interests during a declared emergency; it does not speak in the traditional and constitutionally significant terms of imposing “duties” or “tariffs,” powers the Constitution assigns to Congress in Article I. Reading IEEPA to permit tariff-setting would transform an emergency sanctions statute into a general trade-and-revenue instrument, a construction that lacks clear textual support and raises a major separation-of-powers concern. Even if § 1702(a)(1)(B) were stretched to cover tariffs, the statute provides no meaningful standard for selecting the rate, scope, or duration of duties, creating the kind of boundless delegation inconsistent with J.W. Hampton, Jr. & Co. v. United States, 276 U.S. 394 (1928), and the nondelegation concerns echoed in Gundy v. United States, 588 U.S. 128 (2019). The political-question argument cannot override the judiciary’s duty to interpret statutory text and enforce Article I limits when the Executive asserts taxing power absent a clear congressional grant.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The text of 50 U.S.C. § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to "regulate" or "prohibit" specified emergency-related transactions involving foreign exchange, banking transfers, and property interests, but it does not speak in the distinct terms Congress traditionally uses to impose customs duties or tariffs—an Article I function. Reading IEEPA to permit tariff-setting would transform an emergency sanctions statute into a broad trade-and-revenue instrument, creating serious separation-of-powers concerns and, if accepted, raising a substantial nondelegation problem because IEEPA supplies no tariff-specific limits comparable to those upheld in J.W. Hampton, Jr. & Co. v. United States. Under Hampton’s intelligible-principle framework, any tariff delegation must be cabined by meaningful standards; § 1702(a)(1)(B) lacks that kind of bounded tariff guidance, making the government’s interpretation both textually strained and constitutionally suspect. The political-question argument cannot eliminate the judiciary’s duty to decide the antecedent statutory question of whether Congress conferred this power in the first place.

Reading that general transactional authority to include tariff-setting would substantially reshape the statute into a broad trade-and-revenue instrument, raising serious separation-of-powers concerns and pushing executive action toward the limits recognized in Youngstown’s framework when the President claims power not clearly conferred by Congress. The government’s political-question argument is unpersuasive because courts can decide the straightforward statutory question without second-guessing foreign-policy judgments, and narrowing constructions are appropriate to avoid unnecessary constitutional problems. Because the statute does not clearly authorize tariffs, I would not reach the alternative nondelegation question under J.W. Hampton or Gundy.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: IEEPA § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “regulate” or “prohibit” specified transactions involving foreign exchange, banking transfers, and property interests during a declared emergency, but it does not speak in the distinct terms Congress uses when it confers tariff/duty authority; reading “regulate” to include imposing customs duties would collapse IEEPA into a general trade-and-revenue statute and create serious statutory-coherence and workability problems given Congress’s separate, detailed tariff schemes. On jurisdiction, this challenge “arises under” IEEPA rather than tariff laws channeling to the CIT, consistent with K Mart’s approach to resolving whether a claim is truly brought under customs/tariff provisions or instead under another substantive statute.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: IEEPA § 1702(a)(1)(B) authorizes the President to “regulate” or “prohibit” certain emergency-related transactions involving foreign exchange, banking transfers, and property interests, but it never speaks in the distinct and historically settled terms Congress uses when it delegates authority to “impose duties” or “tariffs” (cf. 19 U.S.C. §§ 1862, 2253, 2411). Given Article I’s assignment of taxing and tariff powers to Congress, I would require a clear statement before reading IEEPA to permit the Executive to levy a charge paid by Americans at the border; the statute’s general verbs cannot silently effect such a major shift in the separation of powers. In United States v.
